title: The Letter to Titus Timeline
sub: Elders for Crete · Sound Doctrine for Every Household
desc: Paul's instructions to Titus, left on Crete to appoint elders and organize churches among a population his own poet called liars and lazy gluttons. Grace, doctrine, and household order run through all three chapters, closing in one of Paul's clearest single statements of salvation by mercy, not works.

eras.label: Era One · Titus 1
eras.name: Appointing Elders on Crete
eras.dates: An island of famously unreliable people, left to Titus to organize into churches with qualified leaders

events.title: Greeting: Apostleship and the Hope of Eternal Life
events.detail: Paul's longest, most doctrinally loaded opening in any of his shorter letters, tying his apostleship directly to a hope promised before time began, now preached on schedule.

verses.text: “The hope of eternal life, which the God who cannot lie promised from all eternity.” — God's own trustworthiness grounds the whole letter's confidence.

events.title: Qualifications for Elders
events.detail: Paul's stated reason for leaving Titus behind: appoint elders in every town, each measured by the same character list Paul gives Timothy: above reproach, hospitable, able to teach and refute error.

verses.text: “Holding fast the faithful word… so that he will be able both to exhort in sound doctrine and to reprove those who contradict.” — an elder's job is defense as much as instruction.

events.title: Silencing the Empty Talkers and Deceivers
events.detail: Paul quotes a Cretan's own poet against his countrymen's reputation, then applies it to the false teachers upsetting whole households for dishonest gain: a sharp, culturally specific rebuke unlike anything in his other letters.

verses.text: “One of themselves, a prophet of their own, said, ‘Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons.’ This testimony is true.” — quoting Epimenides, a 6th-century BC Cretan poet, against his own people.

eras.label: Era Two · Titus 2
eras.name: Sound Doctrine for Every Household
eras.dates: Age, sex, and social station each get their own instruction, all of it aimed at making the gospel look good to outsiders

events.title: Instructions for Older Men, Older Women, the Young, and Titus Himself
events.detail: A household code addressed group by group: older men, older women (who are to teach the younger women), young men, and finally Titus, told to be a living model of what he teaches.

verses.text: “In all things show yourself to be a model of good works… so that the opponent will be put to shame, having nothing bad to say about us.” — Titus's own conduct is itself an apologetic.

events.title: Instructions to Slaves
events.detail: The shortest of the household instructions, but pointed: a slave's honesty and submission is framed as something that can 'adorn' or beautify the doctrine of God in the eyes of a watching household.

verses.text: “Demonstrating all good faith so that they will adorn the doctrine of God our Savior in everything.” — ordinary faithfulness as visible evidence for the gospel.

events.title: The Grace That Trains Us, Waiting for the Blessed Hope
events.detail: The theological hinge of the letter: grace isn't just pardon, it is pictured as a teacher, actively training believers toward godly living while they wait for Christ's appearing.

verses.text: “The grace of God has appeared… instructing us that, denying ungodliness and worldly desires, we should live sensibly, righteously, and godly.” — grace as active trainer, not passive excuse.

“Who gave Himself for us that He might redeem us from all lawlessness, and purify for Himself a people for His own possession, zealous for good works.” — the purpose clause driving the whole letter's ethic.

eras.label: Era Three · Titus 3
eras.name: Saved to Do Good Works
eras.dates: A summary of the gospel bracketed by two lists of good works: grace produces them, it doesn't earn them

events.title: Reminder: Civic Obedience and Gentleness
events.detail: A brief instruction to submit to civic authorities and be peaceable toward everyone, setting up the contrast with what believers themselves used to be, in the next paragraph.

verses.text: “To slander no one, to be peaceable, considerate, demonstrating all gentleness to all men.” — gentleness extended even to a hostile culture.

events.title: Saved by Mercy, Not by Works
events.detail: The letter's fullest gospel summary: believers were once foolish and enslaved to their own desires, and were saved purely by God's mercy through the Spirit's renewal, not by anything they did.

verses.text: “He saved us, not by works which we did in righteousness, but according to His mercy, through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit.” — the clearest single statement of salvation by grace in the letter.

events.title: Good Works, Not Foolish Controversies
events.detail: Having just said works don't save, Paul immediately insists the saved devote themselves to good works, while steering clear of genealogical disputes and factious troublemakers.

verses.text: “Avoid foolish controversies and genealogies and strife and conflicts about the Law, for they are unprofitable and worthless.” — the same Jewish-myth concerns raised back in 1:14.

events.title: Travel Plans and Closing Greetings
events.detail: Practical closing business: Paul plans to winter in Nicopolis, asks Titus to send Zenas and Apollos on their way, and signs off with a final push toward good works.

verses.text: “Our people must also learn to lead in good works to meet pressing needs, so that they will not be unfruitful.” — the letter's last word circles back to its central theme.
